content: Chlorpromazine, developed in the 1950s, continues to be a standard treatment for individuals with schizophrenia. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of chlorpromazine compared to placebo in treating schizophrenia. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared chlorpromazine with placebo in individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia or other serious, chronic mental illnesses. The primary outcomes assessed were death, violent behaviors, overall improvement, relapse, and satisfaction with care. Data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Continuous data were excluded if more than 50% of participants were lost to follow-up. A fixed-effect model was used for analysis. The review examined over 1,100 electronic records, ultimately including 55 studies and excluding 315. The quality of the evidence was rated as very low. Chlorpromazine was found to reduce the number of participants experiencing a relapse compared to placebo during six months to two years of follow-up (n=512, 3 RCTs, RR 0.65, CI 0.47 to 0.90), although the data were heterogeneous. No significant differences in relapse rates were observed in the short, medium, or long term over two years, and these data were also heterogeneous. Chlorpromazine demonstrated a global improvement in symptoms and functioning (n=1164, 14 RCTs, RR 0.71, CI 0.58 to 0.86). Fewer participants assigned to chlorpromazine discontinued trials early compared to placebo (n=1831, 27 RCTs, RR 0.64, CI 0.53 to 0.78). However, chlorpromazine was associated with numerous adverse effects. It was clearly sedating (n=1627, 23 RCTs, RR 2.79, CI 2.25 to 3.45) and increased the likelihood of acute movement disorders (n=942, 5 RCTs, RR 3.47, CI 1.50 to 8.03) and parkinsonism (n=1468, 15 RCTs, RR 2.11, CI 1.59 to 2.80). Akathisia did not occur more frequently in the chlorpromazine group compared to placebo. Chlorpromazine also caused a significant lowering of blood pressure, often accompanied by dizziness (n=1488, 18 RCTs, RR 2.38, CI 1.74 to 3.25), and led to considerable weight gain (n=165, 5 RCTs, RR 4.92, CI 2.32 to 10.43). The authors concluded that the findings of this review largely confirm what clinicians and patients already know about chlorpromazine. While it remains a globally recognized benchmark treatment for psychoses, it is not without its imperfections. The evidence provided in this review should support more informed, evidence-based decision-making by clinicians, caregivers, and patients.
